newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico energy reserves up, petrochem sale on.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico energy reserves up, petrochem sale on.

text.p: Mexico's Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles said Wednesday that hydrocarbon reserves in the country's offshore production region were above expected levels, according to recent studies in the area.

"We have already done calculations for reserves in the marine region and will continue doing studies for the next three years. The results not only confirm reserve levels, but in some cases are more than expected," he told reporters at a year-end gathering.
With current advanced technological exploration devices, Mexico should also be able to better exploit existing oil fields, Reyes said.
State-owned oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) plans to invest 8.143 billion pesos on expanding the offshore Cantarell field, Pemex's largest crude oil and natural gas source.
In 1994, the field yielded 961,000 barrels per day of crude and 416 million cubic feet per day of natural gas.
Reyes said the year-long reserve studies show no new fields have been uncovered, but that "some of the fields are under-explored."
Results from the studies will be made public in January, he said.

In the next month the government is also expected to shed light on its petrochemical sale plan. Last week Pemex's board of directors approved the creation of 10 subsidiary companies corresponding to 10 major petrochemical plants, a preliminary move to allow private minority ownership in exisisting plants.
Any new petrochemical plants can be fully owned by companies, according to the government's partial privatization scheme.
"The goal for next year, now that the strategy is defined, is to reexamine priorities, first and foremost that (the petrochemical industry) grow and grow rapidly," Reyes said.
He said the Energy Ministry has already heard from companies interested in owning part of or one of the new petrochemical companies.
In addition, the ministry plans to launch a campaign early next year to make Mexicans aware of energy alternatives, specifically natural gas.

Natural gas is not yet commonly used in the center and south of the country, but is used along the border with the United States, where natural gas is imported. Authorities hope privatizations in progress for the distribution of natural gas in certain metropolitan areas will boost use of the fuel.
Currently nearly all Mexican residents use liquid petroleum gas, while cleaner burning natural gas is expected to spread through the new distribution systems for industrial use.
"The campaign is so that people not only know what natural gas is, but begin asking for it," Reyes said.
The energy minister also said long-awaited plans to manage Pemex more like a private company are still being considered and are a priority.
"There has been difficulty making Pemex a more international company," he said, noting that mandatory government revision of international projects impedes the company.
Reyes said a more autonomous Pemex should make the company more efficient and competitive. Pemex revenue would continue to be directed to federal coffers in the same amounts, he added.
